arml-2006-power-01a.title: The crease is the perpendicular bisector
arml-2006-power-01a.body: Folding the paper so that $P$ lands on $Q$ reflects the plane in the crease, so the crease is the line of reflection sending $P$ to $Q$: the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{PQ}$.

arml-2006-power-01b.title: Reflection swapping the lines
arml-2006-power-01b.body: A fold taking $\ell_1$ onto $\ell_2$ is a reflection in the crease that swaps the two lines, so the crease passes through their intersection $P$ and bisects the angle between them. It is one of the two angle bisectors of the pair of lines (the two bisectors are perpendicular; the choice depends on how the paper is folded).

arml-2006-power-01c.title: Circle centered at $Q$
arml-2006-power-01c.body:
Suppose a fold puts $P$ at the point $P'$ on $\ell$, with the crease passing through $Q$. The crease is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{PP'}$ (Problem 1a), and $Q$ lies on it, so $QP=QP'$. Hence $P'$ lies on the circle with center $Q$ and radius $QP$, and also on line $\ell$.

Conversely, every point $P'$ where this circle meets $\ell$ gives a fold: fold $P$ onto $P'$ (B2); its crease is the perpendicular bisector of $PP'$, which passes through $Q$ since $QP=QP'$. So the possible folds correspond to the intersection points of the line $\ell$ with the circle of center $Q$ and radius $QP$ (there are $0$, $1$ or $2$ of them).

arml-2006-power-02a.title: Take both lines equal
arml-2006-power-02a.body: B6 does not require $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ to be distinct; in the case $\ell_1=\ell_2=\ell$ the fold simply places both points $P$ and $Q$ onto the line $\ell$. Now, given two lines $a$ and $b$ that we want to fold together (B3), mark two distinct points $P$ and $Q$ arbitrarily on $a$ and apply B6 with the lines $b$ and $b$: it folds $P$ onto $b$ and $Q$ onto $b$. Since $P$ and $Q$ determine the line $a$, the fold places the whole line $a$ onto $b$. This is exactly B3.

arml-2006-power-02b.title: Circle misses the line
arml-2006-power-02b.body: By Problem 1c, a fold exists iff the circle with center $Q$ and radius $QP$ meets $\ell$. Take $P$ and $Q$ on the same side of $\ell$ with $QP$ smaller than the distance from $Q$ to $\ell$. Then the whole circle (of radius $QP$) lies strictly on one side of $\ell$ and does not meet it, so there is no point $P'\in\ell$ with $QP'=QP$, and hence no such fold.

arml-2006-power-03a.title: Two midline folds
arml-2006-power-03a.body:
Use B2 to fold $A$ onto $B$. By Problem 1a the crease is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$, hence also the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{CD}$ (the square's opposite sides are parallel and equal). Call its intersections with $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ $S_1$ and $S_2$: $AS_1S_2D$ has three right angles, so it is a rectangle and $AS_1=DS_2=\frac12$.

Similarly, use B2 to fold $A$ onto $D$: the crease is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AD}$ and of $\overline{BC}$, meeting $AD$ and $BC$ at $T_1$ and $T_2$. Let $M$ be the intersection of the two creases. Then $AS_1MT_1$ has three right angles, so it is a rectangle with $AS_1=\frac12=AT_1$: a square of area $\frac14$. By the same reasoning the other three small quadrilaterals are squares of side $\frac12$, so the two creases divide the unit square into four squares of area $\frac14$.

arml-2006-power-03b.title: Find the center, then fold the corners in
arml-2006-power-03b.body:
To locate the center, use B1 (or B2) on the diagonally opposite corners $A$ and $C$ and then again on $B$ and $D$: with B1 the creases are the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$, which meet at the center. (If B2 is used, the creases are the perpendicular bisectors of $AC$ and $BD$, which are the other diagonals; either way their intersection is the center.) With the center located, use B2 four times to fold each of the corners onto the center. The creases form a square whose vertices are the midpoints of the sides, of area $\frac12$.

Alternatively, without locating the center: use B2 as in 3a to locate the midpoint of each side, and then use B1 on each pair of adjacent midpoints $P$, $Q$. Folding along $PQ$ folds each corner onto the center.

arml-2006-power-04.title: Repeated halving, then folding back strips
arml-2006-power-04.body:
The Meno construction applied to a square of side $s$ gives a square of side $\frac s{\sqrt2}$ and area $\frac{s^2}2$. The Quarter construction gives a square of side $\frac s2$ and area $\frac{s^2}4$. Doing the Meno construction twice is equivalent to doing the Quarter construction once, as the diagram of the original solution shows (folding $ABCD$ into $EFGH$). So each step multiplies the area by $\frac12$ or $\frac14$, and by induction the possible areas of the smallest square are $\frac1{2^n}$ for $n\ge0$.

Smaller squares can also be combined into larger ones by folding back strips along two adjacent edges; for instance, folding back strips of width $\frac14$ at two adjacent sides of the unit square produces a square of side $\frac34$ and area $\frac9{16}$. Therefore the possible areas are of the form $\dfrac{k^2}{2^n}$, where $k\le2^{n/2}$. Constructions that need creases other than those of Quarter and Meno constructions (such as a tilted square of area $\frac{10}{16}$) are not allowed.

arml-2006-power-05a.title: Count strings
arml-2006-power-05a.body:
Each Meno multiplies the area by $\frac12$ and each Quarter by $\frac14=\frac1{2^2}$. A way of obtaining area $\frac1{2^n}$ is a string of letters M and Q in which M counts $1$ and Q counts $2$ with total $n$.

| $n$ | strings | count |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | M | 1 |
| 2 | Q, MM | 2 |
| 3 | QM, MQ, MMM | 3 |
| 4 | QQ, QMM, MQM, MMQ, MMMM | 5 |
| 5 | QQM, QMQ, MQQ, QMMM, MQMM, MMQM, MMMQ, MMMMM | 8 |
| 6 | QQQ, QQMM, QMQM, QMMQ, MQQM, MQMQ, MMQQ, QMMMM, MQMMM, MMQMM, MMMQM, MMMMQ, MMMMMM | 13 |

So the numbers of ways are $1,2,3,5,8,13$.

arml-2006-power-05b.title: Fibonacci recursion
arml-2006-power-05b.body:
Let $W_n$ be the set of all strings in $\{M,Q\}$ producing area $\frac1{2^n}$ (M counts $1$, Q counts $2$), and $F(n)=|W_n|$. A string for $n+1$ ends either in Q (and the rest is a string for $n-1$) or in M (and the rest is a string for $n$):
$$W_{n+1}=\{xQ: x\in W_{n-1}\}\ \cup\ \{yM: y\in W_n\}.$$
The two sets are disjoint because the strings in the first end in Q and in the second in M. Hence $F(n+1)=F(n-1)+F(n)$. With $F(0)=1$ (the empty string) and $F(1)=1$ (M), $F(n)=f_{n+1}$ where $f_1=f_2=1$, $f_{k+2}=f_{k+1}+f_k$ is the Fibonacci sequence. ∎

arml-2006-power-06a.title: Parallel creases cut equal segments
arml-2006-power-06a.body:
Let the square be $ABCD$ with $AB$ the bottom side and $D$ above $A$.

1. Using B2, fold $D$ onto $A$ and unfold; the crease passes through the midpoint $M$ of $\overline{AD}$ and is perpendicular to $\overline{AD}$ (Problem 3a).
2. Use B2 again to fold $M$ onto $A$ and onto $D$; the creases are perpendicular to $\overline{AD}$ through the midpoints $P$ of $\overline{MA}$ and $N$ of $\overline{MD}$. Now the creases through $P$, $M$, $N$ are at heights $\frac14,\frac12,\frac34$ above $A$. Let $\overline{NR}$ be the crease through $N$ (with $R$ on $\overline{BC}$).
3. Use B5: fold $B$ up onto line $NR$ with the crease passing through $A$. Let $B'$ be the image of $B$. Then $AB'=AB=1$ and $B'$ is at height $\frac34$.
4. Let $T_1'$ and $T_2'$ be the points where the creases through $P$ (height $\frac14$) and $M$ (height $\frac12$) cross $\overline{AB'}$.

*Justification.* The creases through $P,M,N$ are all perpendicular to $\overline{AD}$, hence parallel, and they cut equal segments $AP=PM=MN$ on the transversal $\overline{AD}$. Parallel lines that cut equal segments on one transversal cut equal segments on any transversal, so they also cut $\overline{AB'}$ into equal pieces: $AT_1'=T_1'T_2'=T_2'B'=\frac13$ (the heights $\frac14,\frac12,\frac34$ are in the ratio $1:2:3$). Finally unfold the B5 fold: reflection in the crease through $A$ takes $B'$ back to $B$ and the segment $\overline{AB'}$ onto $\overline{AB}$, so the images $T_1,T_2$ of $T_1',T_2'$ trisect $\overline{AB}$.

arml-2006-power-06b.title: Equally spaced parallel creases
arml-2006-power-06b.body:
Let $k=n$. Choose $m$ with $2^m>k$ and repeatedly bisect $\overline{AD}$ a total of $m$ times (using B2 as in 3a), producing $2^m-1$ parallel creases perpendicular to $AD$ (each is perpendicular to $AD$ by 3a) that are equally spaced along $AD$ with spacing $\frac1{2^m}$. Unfold, and using B5 fold vertex $B$ up to the $k$th crease (counting from $A$) so that the new crease passes through $A$. Let $B'$ be the image of $B$: it lies on the $k$th crease, so $AB'$ meets the first $k-1$ creases. The intersections of the lower creases with $\overline{AB'}$ divide $\overline{AB'}$ into $k$ equal segments, since the parallel creases are equally spaced (equal intercepts on the transversal $AD$ give equal intercepts on $AB'$). Fold back to move these points to side $AB$ if desired.

Alternatively, pick an arbitrary point $M_1$ on $\overline{AD}$ very near $A$, fold a perpendicular to $AD$ through $M_1$ with B4, let $M_2$ be the image of $A$ under the fold (B2 gives the equal spacing $AM_1=M_1M_2$), and continue folding perpendiculars through successive points, so that $k$ equally spaced parallel creases are obtained ($M_1$ must satisfy $AM_1\le\frac1k$ so there is room for all $k$ folds), then proceed as above.

arml-2006-power-07.title: Sides $m/n$ and the Meno construction
arml-2006-power-07.body:
By Problem 6 the sides of the square can be divided into $n$ equal pieces for any $n\ge1$ (for $n=1,2$ trivially or by the Quarter construction). So sides of length $\frac mn$ with $1\le m\le n$ can be marked.

To obtain a square of side $\frac mn$: use the construction of Problem 6 to mark the point $P$ that is $\frac mn$ of the way from $A$ to $B$. Use B3 to find the corresponding point $Q$ on $\overline{AD}$ (fold $AB$ onto $AD$ so that $P$ lands on $AD$). At both $P$ and $Q$ use B4 to create a crease perpendicular to the respective side of $ABCD$. The two creases meet at a point $R$, and $APRQ$ is a square of side $\frac mn$ and area $\left(\frac mn\right)^2=\frac{m^2}{n^2}$.

The Meno construction applied to the square $APRQ$ halves its area, giving $\dfrac{m^2}{2n^2}$.

So every fraction of the form $\dfrac{m^2}{n^2}$ or $\dfrac{m^2}{2n^2}$ (with integers $1\le m\le n$) can be obtained as the area of a folded square.

arml-2006-power-08a.title: Geometric mean
arml-2006-power-08a.body:
First fold a crease $\ell$ through $B$ with $\ell\perp BC$ using B4. Unfold and fold $A$ onto $C$ using B2; let $O$ be the midpoint of $\overline{AC}$ determined by this crease. Unfold and fold $C$ onto $\ell$ with the crease passing through $O$ using B5 (the circle centered at $O$ of radius $OC$ meets $\ell$). Let $C'$ be the image of $C$ on the crease $\ell$.

Now $OC=\frac{AC}2$ by B2, and $OC'=OC$ by construction, so $C'$ lies on the circle with diameter $\overline{AC}$. Since $\overline{BC'}\perp\overline{AC}$ by construction, $BC'$ is the geometric mean of $AB$ and $BC$ (the altitude to the hypotenuse in a right triangle $AC'C$): $(BC')^2=AB\cdot BC=1\cdot r=r$, so $BC'=\sqrt r$.

arml-2006-power-08b.title: Circle centered at the midpoint of $\overline{BE}$
arml-2006-power-08b.body:
Fold point $B$ onto $E$ using B2 and mark the midpoint $F$ of $\overline{BE}$. Then $EF=\frac{1-r}2$ and $AF=r+\frac{1-r}2=\frac{r+1}2$.

Using B4, fold a crease $\ell$ through $E$ perpendicular to $\overline{AB}$. Using B5, fold $A$ onto $\ell$ with the crease passing through $F$ (possible because the circle with center $F$ and radius $FA=\frac{1+r}2$ meets $\ell$, as $\frac{1+r}2>EF$). Let $A'$ be the image of $A$ on $\ell$; then $A'F=AF=\frac{r+1}2$. In the right triangle $A'EF$,
$$(A'E)^2=\left(\frac{r+1}2\right)^2-\left(\frac{1-r}2\right)^2=r,$$
so $A'E=\sqrt r$, and the segment $\overline{EA'}$ lies inside the unit square (it is along $\ell$, of length $\sqrt r<1$).

arml-2006-power-09.title: Square roots of rational lengths
arml-2006-power-09.body:
Using Problems 6 and 7, any side length of the form $\frac kn$ ($1\le k\le n$) can be constructed on the square. By Problem 8b, from a length $r<1$ one can construct a length $\sqrt r$, so any side length of the form $\sqrt{\frac kn}$ can be constructed, i.e. a square of area $\frac kn$ exactly: take $r=\frac kn$, build the segment of length $\sqrt{k/n}$ inside the unit square, and make it the side of a folded square (as in Problem 7: use B3 and B4 at the endpoints). Therefore every area $\dfrac kn$ with $1\le k\le n$ can be obtained.

Better still, taking square roots repeatedly: from $\frac kn$ we can build a side $\sqrt[4]{\frac kn}$ and an area $\sqrt{\frac kn}$, and in general areas of the form $\left(\frac kn\right)^{1/2^m}$, by repeated application of 8b. In particular, an area of $\frac{\sqrt2}2=\sqrt{\frac12}$ is possible.

arml-2006-power-10a.title: Altitude of an equilateral triangle
arml-2006-power-10a.body:
The altitude of a unit equilateral triangle is $\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and gives a square of area $\frac34$.

1. Fold $A$ onto $B$ using B2 and mark the midpoint $E$ of $\overline{AB}$ on the crease; the crease through $E$ is perpendicular to $\overline{AB}$.
2. Fold $D$ onto the crease through $E$ with the new crease passing through $A$ (B5). Let $D'$ be the image of $D$ on the first crease. Then $AD'=AD=1$, $AE=\frac12$ and $\angle AED'=90^\circ$, so $ED'=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.
3. Using B4, fold a crease through $D'$ perpendicular to $\overline{ED'}$; it is parallel to $\overline{AB}$ and meets $\overline{AD}$ at a point $F$ with $AF=ED'=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.
4. Using B3, fold $\overline{AD}$ onto $\overline{AB}$ and mark the image $F'$ of $F$ on $\overline{AB}$: $AF'=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.
5. Using B4, fold a perpendicular to $\overline{AB}$ at $F'$; let $H$ be its intersection with the crease from step 3.

Then $A$, $F'$, $H$, $F$ are the vertices of a square of side $\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and area $\frac34$, obtained in $5$ folds.

arml-2006-power-10b.title: Four creases from the vertices to midpoints
arml-2006-power-10b.body:
Let $ABCD$ be the unit square. Using B2, fold $A$ onto $B$ (crease through the midpoints $E$ of $\overline{AB}$ and $G$ of $\overline{CD}$) and fold $A$ onto $D$ (crease through the midpoints $H$ of $\overline{AD}$ and $F$ of $\overline{BC}$): $2$ folds. Then use B1 four times to crease the lines $AF$, $BG$, $CH$ and $DE$: $4$ more folds, $6$ folds in all.

The four creases bound a square. With $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(1,1)$, $D=(0,1)$ we have $F=(1,\frac12)$, $G=(\frac12,1)$, $H=(0,\frac12)$, $E=(\frac12,0)$ and the lines
$$AF:\ y=\tfrac x2,\quad BG:\ y=2-2x,\quad CH:\ y=\tfrac12+\tfrac x2,\quad DE:\ y=1-2x.$$
Their intersections (consecutive pairs) are $\left(\frac25,\frac15\right)$, $\left(\frac45,\frac25\right)$, $\left(\frac35,\frac45\right)$, $\left(\frac15,\frac35\right)$. Consecutive vertices differ by $\left(\frac25,\frac15\right)$ rotated by $90^\circ$ each time, so the figure is a square of side $\sqrt{\frac4{25}+\frac1{25}}=\frac{\sqrt5}5$ and area $\frac15$. This needs only $6$ folds (fewer than $12$; the official solution gives a $10$-fold construction).
